extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Horace/classical Latin literature; readers interested in satirical poetry and Roman moral commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical commentary on themes, tone, and ethical prescriptions in Horace's Satires (esp. mutual forbearance, satirical tone, and choice of subjects). Useful for composing or interpreting Horatian-style satire and moralizing poetic prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination before criticizing
rubrics_metrics.description: A man should examine himself and search out his own faults before criticizing others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Maenius (who carped at Novius yet 'egomet mi ignosco'): self-satisfaction that notices others' faults while overlooking one's own is foolish and deserves censure. The text urges personal scrutiny (burn the bracken that springs up in neglected fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual forbearance and discrimination of failings
rubrics_metrics.description: We should be indulgent to the weaknesses of our friends and discriminate between mere impropriety and heinous crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship requires tolerance: do not treat every failing equally; exercise judgment in assigning blame (a mere impropriety is not as serious as a heinous crime). The passage explicitly rejects the Stoic paradox that 'all offences are equal' as contrary to common sense and social evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindly, genial satirical tone (avoid over-censoriousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire should often be kindly and genial in tone rather than harshly censorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary notes Satire III's milder tone (contrast with Lucilian invective) and suggests Horace may soften his tone when his circumstances (e.g., acquaintance with Maecenas) improve. The aim is to disarm criticism rather than to rage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh virtues against faults (reciprocal indulgence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging a friend, weigh his virtues against his faults and, if virtues prevail, incline to love and pardon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied reciprocity: one who asks pardon for faults deserves that his friend return indulgence for comparable faults; 'one who craves indulgence for failings should grant it in return.' Practical moral measure: balance objects on the same scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional justice / punishments suited to offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason should punish offences proportionately; do not treat all sins as identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lampoons extreme punishments (e.g., crucifying a slave for taking a half-eaten fish) and argues for measured penalties fitted to the gravity of the crime rather than universal equality of sins (rejecting the Stoic 'omnia peccata paria').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer transparent/frank partners to concealed ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer those who openly show what they are (courtesans) to those who conceal faults (matrons), to avoid deception and peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to buying horses (inspecting covered animals): courtesans 'present their wares without disguise' whereas matrons hide defects under robes, leading to reputational and practical risks. Transparency reduces the chance of being deceived and extorted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose easy, attainable pleasures (moderation in desires)
rubrics_metrics.description: Love and pleasure should be chosen to be easy and attainable rather than costly, slow, or extravagant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted Philodemus: prefer a woman who is neither high-priced nor slow to come; the speaker values an accessible, modest partner—an aesthetic of parability and simplicity over lavish, risky pursuits. Also tied to Epicurean inquiry into limits of desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid courting matrons (prudence about risks to reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pursuing married, high-born women (matrons), since association with them brings greater pain and reputational ruin than liaison with courtesans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of severe consequences (men flogged, killed, mutilated, or disgraced) and historical anecdotes (Villius and Fausta) illustrate the practical and social hazards of adulterous intrigues with matrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask nature's limits; practise temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on the limits nature assigns to desires and practise temperance rather than indulging insatiable wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical questions (seek golden cups when thirsty?) and Epicurean references (void vs. solid) urge assessment of what will satisfy versus what will cause pain—advocating moderation and avoidance of needless excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid exempla and contrasts to satirize foibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire employs concrete examples of inconsistency and contrast (e.g., Tigellius' extremes) to expose human foibles and hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tigellius is used as a foil (inconsistency of speech and behavior, lavish talk then begging simplicity) to ridicule and illuminate broader human weaknesses; exempla and comic detail enhance satirical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship: affectionate tolerance and reframing faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat friends with the tenderness of a father to a child: tolerate blemishes and reframe defects with affectionate nicknames rather than scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of pet-names (Blinky, Chickabiddy, Cruikshank) show how endearment neutralizes defects; the social practice of reframing faults fosters and preserves friendships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and preserve true virtues (do not invert them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid inverting virtues into faults—do not label modesty as stupidity, simplicity as boorishness, or prudence as craftiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes social tendency to misname virtues and urges proper appreciation of qualities such as honesty, sobriety, simplicity, and prudence; this is part of maintaining sincere social bonds and proper moral judgment.
